params.eyebrow: Paper analysis · dense prediction × continuous thought
params.headline: Compact thought collides with dense output

beats.intent: Name the tension the paper is about.
beats.narration: This paper puts a thought process that stays small up against a task whose output has to stay large — every pixel of it.

params.headline: One pass in, one pass out, and a loop in the middle
params.note: Parameters are shared across every tick.

beats.intent: The recurrence sits after the encoder, not around it.
beats.narration: The encoder does the heavy lifting first, in the style SwinIR established. Then the field is cut into windows, and nothing is pooled away on the way through. The thought machine sits here in the middle, working on what the windows hold. Only at the very end does the decoder upsample, four times over. That loop is a single tick, and it runs in place rather than around the whole pipeline. Every tick reuses the same weights, so thinking for longer costs time and not memory.

params.headline: Every window keeps its own position-wise query

beats.intent: DQ-CTM produces one query per position, not one per window.
beats.narration: The three approaches sit side by side here, and they differ only in what they hand the thought block. The windows come first: the field is partitioned, and each one is handled on its own. The block in the middle is shared, the same weights for every window. And what comes out is still a dense field, one query for every position in it.

params.headline: Attention is computed inside windows, and no token is pooled away
params.note: Token count is identical before and after the update.

beats.intent: The carrier keeps every position across ticks.
beats.narration: Picture the feature map as a grid of tokens. Attention runs inside one window at a time. The next window does the same, and at this stage the two never mix. Count the tokens before a tick and after it and you get the same number.

params.headline: The encoder makes the field; the partition keeps it

terms.label: SwinIR-style encoder — LR in, dense feature field out
window partition — every token survives it

beats.intent: Encoding and partitioning, with nothing discarded.
beats.narration: The encoder turns the low-resolution image into a dense feature field. The partition then cuts that field into windows without throwing any of it away.

params.headline: The thought state is a stack the carrier is read through

beats.intent: The compact state never replaces the dense carrier.
beats.narration: At the bottom is the carrier, and it keeps every token it started with. Above it sit the queries — one for each position, rather than one for each window. Synchronisation is the part that remembers: every neuron carries its own history. The compact state on top is what actually changes from one tick to the next.

params.headline: One summary token per window, or one query per pixel
params.note: Same window partition; different interface to the thought state.

beats.intent: The contrast that names the contribution.
beats.narration: The window-wise version collapses each window down to a single summary token. This one asks a question at every position instead, and the token count survives it. The partition is identical in both. What differs is how much of it the thought state ever sees.

params.headline: The method is mid-pack on parameters, not the smallest
params.note: Smaller is better; DQ-CTM-SR is second largest here.

beats.intent: Where the method sits on cost.
beats.narration: On parameters the method is the second largest here, at 1.13 million. So this is not the cheap option, and the paper never claims it is.
